documents.text:
Donghua Hang

Donghua Hang is a renowned researcher in the field of animal science, best known for his contributions to the study of animal behavior and welfare. Early Life and Education

Donghua Hang was born on February 12, 1975, in Beijing, China. He received his Bachelor's degree in Biology from Peking University in 1997. Hang then pursued his graduate studies at the University of Cambridge, where he earned his Ph.D. in Animal Behavior in 2002. Career

After completing his Ph.D., Hang joined the Institute of Animal Science in Prague, Czech Republic, as a postdoctoral researcher. During his tenure at the institute, he worked under the guidance of Dr. Eva Nováková, a prominent expert in animal welfare. Hang's research focused on the behavioral responses of farm animals to different environmental stimuli. Studies and Research

One of Hang's most notable studies, published in the Journal of Animal Science in 2005, investigated the effects of enrichment strategies on the behavior of pigs in intensive farming systems. [1] The study found that providing pigs with access to toys and puzzle feeders significantly reduced stress and aggression, leading to improved welfare outcomes. In 2007, Hang collaborated with a team of researchers from the University of Veterinary and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Brno, Czech Republic, to investigate the impact of housing systems on the behavior and welfare of laying hens. [2] The study's findings highlighted the importance of providing hens with adequate space and opportunities for foraging and dust bathing. In 2010, Hang was appointed as a senior researcher at the Institute of Animal Science, where he continued to conduct research on animal behavior and welfare. His work has been cited over 500 times, according to Google Scholar. References

[1] Hang, D. (2005). "The effects of enrichment strategies on the behavior of pigs in intensive farming systems." Journal of Animal Science, 83(10), 2511-2518. [2] Nováková, E., Hang, D., & Šťastný, K. (2007). "The impact of housing systems on the behavior and welfare of laying hens." Animal Welfare, 16(2), 147-155.
